1. A nation's sovereignty — its right to govern itself without outside interference — is the foundation of the current world order. --- SOVEREIGNTY (n) = chủ quyền quốc gia; "national sovereignty", "respect/violate sovereignty".

2. An international body can impose economic sanctions on a state to force it to change its behaviour. --- SANCTIONS (n, luôn số nhiều với nghĩa trừng phạt) = lệnh trừng phạt; "impose/lift economic sanctions".

3. Several officials were found guilty of embezzlement after secretly diverting large sums of relief money entrusted to them. --- EMBEZZLEMENT (n) = biển thủ, tham ô công quỹ được giao phó; "embezzlement of funds", "charged with embezzlement".

4. Only multilateral cooperation, involving many countries at once, can realistically tackle a crisis of this scale. --- MULTILATERAL (adj) = đa phương (3+ bên); "multilateral cooperation/treaty/negotiations".
5. Once enough governments have ratified it, the treaty will become legally binding. --- RATIFY (v) = phê chuẩn chính thức (hiệp ước/thoả thuận); "ratify a treaty", "await ratification".

6. Donor organisations are under growing pressure to demonstrate accountability for exactly how relief funds are spent. --- ACCOUNTABILITY (n, không đếm được) = trách nhiệm giải trình; "international accountability", "hold someone accountable".
7. Years of aid dependency can leave a country's own industries unable to compete on their own. --- DEPENDENCY (n) = sự lệ thuộc kéo dài (vào viện trợ); "aid dependency", "a cycle of dependency".

8. International courts only have jurisdiction to try certain crimes when specific conditions are met. --- JURISDICTION (n) = thẩm quyền tài phán; "fall under the jurisdiction of", "universal jurisdiction".

9. Some powerful individuals seem able to act with impunity, committing serious wrongdoing without ever facing punishment. --- IMPUNITY (n) = sự không bị trừng phạt; "act with impunity", "a culture of impunity".

10. The Responsibility to Protect — the doctrine holding that the world has a duty to step in when a government fails to protect its own people — was formally endorsed in 2005. --- RESPONSIBILITY TO PROTECT (noun phrase, viết hoa, viết tắt "R2P") = Trách nhiệm Bảo vệ; "invoke/endorse the Responsibility to Protect".

11. Diplomats and aid workers alike continue to grapple with the difficult question of when outside intervention is justified. --- GRAPPLE WITH (phrasal verb, luôn đi kèm "with") = vật lộn, nỗ lực giải quyết (vấn đề khó); "grapple with a challenge/an issue".

passages.text: For most of the second half of the twentieth century, international development economics relied on country-level statistics: aggregate growth rates, capital flows and overall poverty headcounts. Whether a particular aid programme had improved the daily lives of the families it targeted was largely a matter of inference rather than direct evidence. Since the early 2000s, two distinct research traditions have tried to put that question on a firmer empirical footing. The first, associated most closely with Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has applied the methods of randomised controlled trials to small-scale interventions. The second, advanced most forcefully by William Easterly of New York University, has examined the macroeconomic record of large aid flows and concluded, broadly, that the news is not good. Neither tradition has displaced the other, and the disagreement between them now shapes much of the published policy advice.

The trial-based approach, sometimes called the J-PAL programme after the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab that Banerjee and Duflo co-founded, treats development questions as if they were medical questions. A programme that hands out free bed nets, deworming tablets or conditional cash transfers is rolled out in some villages but not in others, with the allocation determined by chance, and outcomes are measured a year or two later. By 2019, when Banerjee, Duflo and Michael Kremer shared the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, the J-PAL network had completed more than a thousand such trials across some sixty countries. The headline finding, on which the laureates themselves have insisted, is modest: small, well-designed programmes can produce measurable improvements in specific outcomes such as school attendance or vaccination rates, but no single programme transforms the wider economy.

Easterly's critique runs along different lines. In a series of books and papers from the mid-2000s onwards, he has argued that the global aid effort, taken as a whole, has spent more than two trillion US dollars over five decades with very little to show for it at the level of national growth. Drawing on cross-country regressions, he has pointed out that the countries which have moved most decisively out of poverty since 1980 — South Korea, Vietnam, Botswana, parts of China — have done so largely on the back of domestic policy reform and trade integration rather than on the back of donor transfers. Easterly is careful to distinguish humanitarian relief, which he regards as straightforwardly defensible, from long-term development aid, where he believes the evidence base is much weaker than donor publications generally admit.

These two positions are not, in principle, contradictory. A specific deworming trial may show clear gains while overall aid flows remain inefficient; equally, aggregate stagnation may mask many individual programmes that work. The difficulty arises when policymakers try to draw conclusions about what to do next. Trial evidence tends to support tightly designed, locally delivered interventions; cross-country evidence tends to support institutional reform inside recipient governments. The two reading lists do not, in practice, sit easily on the same desk.

A related debate has unfolded around microfinance, once celebrated as a magic ingredient in poverty reduction. Six randomised evaluations conducted between 2009 and 2015 in India, Mexico, Mongolia, Morocco, Bosnia and Ethiopia, summarised by the American Economic Association, found that access to small loans tended to increase business investment by existing entrepreneurs but produced little measurable effect on average household income or on women's empowerment within twelve to twenty-four months. The findings were widely interpreted as a corrective to earlier, more enthusiastic claims, although several of the original researchers have argued that the time horizons were too short to capture longer-run effects.

Where does this leave policy? Two more recent contributions have attempted a partial synthesis. Nancy Birdsall of the Center for Global Development has argued that the trial literature is most useful precisely where Easterly is most sceptical: in identifying which individual programmes, among the very many funded, are worth scaling. The aggregate disappointment Easterly documents, on this reading, partly reflects the dilution of effective interventions by ineffective ones. From a different angle, Lant Pritchett, formerly at the Harvard Kennedy School, has cautioned that trials work best for narrow, measurable outcomes but cannot adjudicate the larger institutional questions — whether tax administration improves, whether courts function — on which long-run development tends to depend. Pritchett's preferred metaphor is that trials provide useful flashlights but a poor map.

Does aid work? The evidence rewards the question only once it is broken into three. Well-designed programmes, monitored and evaluated, can deliver real benefits to the families they reach. Large transfers to poorly governed states tend, on the whole, to produce less reliable returns. And the institutional reforms that matter most for long-run growth lie largely outside the reach of any single donor agency. The interesting policy question, taken together, is therefore not whether to give but how to divide a budget across these three quite different uses — and whether agencies built for one of them can plausibly be reconfigured for the others.

content.title: Advanced Reading Lesson T19 — International Aid Effectiveness (Advanced)

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture extends our development-economics series — focusing on the empirical literature concerning the effectiveness of bilateral development assistance in low-income recipient states. [pause:5s] The conceptual scaffolding I'll draw on is taken from the work of Professor Solene Kowalczyk — that's K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K, no apostrophe, no umlaut. Kowalczyk's 2014 monograph reframed aid effectiveness from a linear input-output model into what she calls "absorptive-capacity theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The longitudinal panel I'll reference today was first compiled in 2003 — sorry, let me correct that, 2001; the published descriptive statistics in 2003 covered data collected in 2001. So whenever I refer to the baseline year, please record 2001. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation note. Kowalczyk's framework USED TO be operationalised using gross disbursement figures only, NOW the field deploys mixed-methods designs incorporating ethnographic ministry-level interviews, and from 2027 a multi-donor consortium WILL be rolling out blockchain-tracked disbursement modules. So past, present, future. For today's purposes I'm focusing on the CURRENT methodological state — that is, mixed-methods. Moving to terminology. The aid concept Kowalczyk foregrounds — a country's structural ability to convert incoming funds into measurable public-service outputs — is termed "absorptive capacity". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: utilisation rate, fund assimilation, disbursement efficiency. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Kowalczyk's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is absorptive capacity — a-b-s-o-r-p-t-i-v-e capacity. So when the older literature uses utilisation rate or disbursement efficiency, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what economists call the "conditionality continuum". When evaluators describe how donor states attach policy strings to aid packages, they sketch a graded continuum running from unconditional grants through performance-tied tranches to fully conditional structural-adjustment programmes. So, you know, you'll see donors who release funds outright with no fiscal demands — that's unconditional. Or donors who tie release to inflation targets — that's performance-tied. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the conditionality continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the panel data — and this is where I want you to pay close attention, because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the sixty-two recipient states we tracked across four decades, MOST showed positive marginal returns to additional aid — roughly seventy-one per cent. Only a few — about eleven per cent — recorded statistically null returns, and some — eighteen per cent — exhibited mixed effects depending on sector. So the marginal-return picture is broadly positive, but the null-effect tail, though small, is theoretically significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "aid fragmentation". This refers to the phenomenon where recipient ministries simultaneously administer disbursements from many small uncoordinated donors, each with separate reporting templates. At the Riverside Health Ministry, our research assistants documented sixty-seven concurrent donor relationships across one budget cycle. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that more aid linearly produces more development is, frankly, not supported. Most of the recipient states in our panel did NOT exhibit the predicted monotonic gain in human-development indices as bilateral aid volume increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a diminishing-returns curve, with marginal benefit declining beyond a threshold of around fifteen per cent of GDP. So the older "more-is-better" hypothesis, which predicts linear gains, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I made at the start. That CURRENT mixed-methods state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in today's seminar this afternoon. I want you to focus on the ethnographic ministry-interview protocols specifically, not the blockchain futures or the legacy disbursement-figure instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: aid effectiveness is a function of absorptive capacity, not a function of volume; the technical term for fund-conversion ability is absorptive capacity; positive marginal returns dominate at roughly seventy-one per cent; and the more-is-better hypothesis is empirically not supported. Next week we'll examine donor coordination architectures. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The two pie charts illustrate how global humanitarian aid was distributed across seven sectors by major OECD donors in 2000 and 2024.

Overall, aid allocation underwent a pronounced reconfiguration: long-term development categories such as education and infrastructure contracted markedly, while climate- and health-related sectors expanded to dominate contemporary donor commitment. This suggests that aid has become increasingly reactive rather than developmental.

To begin with, climate adaptation surged sixfold from a marginal 3% to 18%, while disbursement to health and pandemic response climbed from 14% to 24%, overtaking food aid to become the single leading sector. Conversely, infrastructure and water funding plummeted from 18% to a mere 4%, the steepest fall of any category, while education's share contracted from 16% to 11%.

Meanwhile, the remaining sectors shifted only modestly. Emergency food and shelter, although still substantial, retreated from 28% to 22%, slipping from first to second place, and governance and anti-corruption funding eased slightly from 9% to 7%. By contrast, refugee and displacement assistance edged up from 12% to 14%, broadly consistent with the protracted displacement crises observed worldwide over the period.

blocks.text: Few questions in international relations are as contentious as whether the outside world should intervene when a government abuses its own people. While some insist that sovereignty is sacrosanct, others argue that universal human rights override territorial borders. My own view, with reservations, is that sovereignty should yield in cases of mass atrocity, although intervention must be tightly disciplined.

On one hand, defenders of strict non-interference tend to argue that respect for sovereignty is what keeps the international order stable. It is precisely because powerful states historically used 'humanitarian' pretexts to invade weaker ones that many developing nations remain deeply suspicious of intervention today. Furthermore, foreign military action, even when well-intentioned, often produces severe repercussions for civilians - refugee waves, embezzlement of relief funds and prolonged instability - outcomes that no donor country can fully control.

On the other hand, advocates of intervention point out that the doctrine of sovereignty was never meant to shield perpetrators of genocide or ethnic cleansing. When a regime turns its weapons on its own citizens, the international community has a moral obligation, arguably codified by the Responsibility to Protect, to step in. Targeted sanctions, peacekeeping missions and multilateral pressure can sometimes halt atrocities without firing a single shot, particularly when authorised by the UN Security Council.

In my view, sovereignty should be respected as the default rule, but it cannot be absolute when grave human rights violations are taking place. Provided that intervention is multilateral, proportionate and aimed at protecting civilians rather than regime change, the international community is justified in acting. Otherwise, sovereignty becomes a shield behind which dictators commit atrocities with impunity.

Humanitarian intervention sits uneasily at the intersection of two competing pillars of international order: the Westphalian principle of sovereignty and the post-1945 codification of universal human rights. While respect for sovereignty remains the default rule, it should, in my view, yield in narrowly defined circumstances where atrocities engage the realm of jus cogens norms.

Defenders of strict non-interference argue that sovereign equality is the load-bearing wall of the international system. Were it abandoned lightly, powerful states would, as history attests, repurpose 'humanitarian' rhetoric to justify regime change in geopolitically convenient locations. So consequential are these precedents that even well-intentioned action can erode trust in multilateral institutions for decades, particularly in the Global South. Moreover, coercive measures - comprehensive sanctions, no-fly zones, military strikes - frequently produce severe repercussions for the very civilians they purport to protect, while dictators absorb the political costs with relative ease.

By contrast, proponents of intervention contend that sovereignty was never designed to shield genocide, ethnic cleansing or crimes against humanity. The Responsibility to Protect doctrine, endorsed by the UN General Assembly in 2005, explicitly conditions sovereignty on a state's discharge of its duty to its population. Where that duty collapses, the international community arguably acquires a residual obligation, exercisable through targeted sanctions, peacekeeping operations and, as a last resort, multilateral force authorised by the Security Council.

My own position is that sovereignty deserves robust protection in ordinary politics but must give way when jus cogens prohibitions are breached on a systematic scale. Provided that intervention is multilaterally authorised, proportionate and tightly framed around civilian protection rather than regime engineering, it can be both lawful and legitimate. Beyond those guardrails, however, sovereignty must be respected, lest humanitarianism degenerate into a polite cover for great-power competition.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. A nation's sovereignty — its right to govern itself without outside interference — is the foundation of the current world order. --- SOVEREIGNTY (n) = chủ quyền quốc gia; "national sovereignty", "respect/violate sovereignty".

2. An international body can impose economic sanctions on a state to force it to change its behaviour. --- SANCTIONS (n, luôn số nhiều với nghĩa trừng phạt) = lệnh trừng phạt; "impose/lift economic sanctions".

3. Several officials were found guilty of embezzlement after secretly diverting large sums of relief money entrusted to them. --- EMBEZZLEMENT (n) = biển thủ, tham ô công quỹ được giao phó; "embezzlement of funds", "charged with embezzlement".

4. Only multilateral cooperation, involving many countries at once, can realistically tackle a crisis of this scale. --- MULTILATERAL (adj) = đa phương (3+ bên); "multilateral cooperation/treaty/negotiations".
5. Once enough governments have ratified it, the treaty will become legally binding. --- RATIFY (v) = phê chuẩn chính thức (hiệp ước/thoả thuận); "ratify a treaty", "await ratification".

6. Donor organisations are under growing pressure to demonstrate accountability for exactly how relief funds are spent. --- ACCOUNTABILITY (n, không đếm được) = trách nhiệm giải trình; "international accountability", "hold someone accountable".
7. Years of aid dependency can leave a country's own industries unable to compete on their own. --- DEPENDENCY (n) = sự lệ thuộc kéo dài (vào viện trợ); "aid dependency", "a cycle of dependency".

8. International courts only have jurisdiction to try certain crimes when specific conditions are met. --- JURISDICTION (n) = thẩm quyền tài phán; "fall under the jurisdiction of", "universal jurisdiction".

9. Some powerful individuals seem able to act with impunity, committing serious wrongdoing without ever facing punishment. --- IMPUNITY (n) = sự không bị trừng phạt; "act with impunity", "a culture of impunity".

10. The Responsibility to Protect — the doctrine holding that the world has a duty to step in when a government fails to protect its own people — was formally endorsed in 2005. --- RESPONSIBILITY TO PROTECT (noun phrase, viết hoa, viết tắt "R2P") = Trách nhiệm Bảo vệ; "invoke/endorse the Responsibility to Protect".

11. Diplomats and aid workers alike continue to grapple with the difficult question of when outside intervention is justified. --- GRAPPLE WITH (phrasal verb, luôn đi kèm "with") = vật lộn, nỗ lực giải quyết (vấn đề khó); "grapple with a challenge/an issue".

12. The tribunal was established specifically to prosecute atrocity crimes, including genocide and crimes against humanity. --- ATROCITY CRIMES (n phrase, thuật ngữ pháp lý cụ thể) = tội ác tày trời; "perpetrate/prosecute atrocity crimes".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Wealthier nations arguably have a moral obligation to provide humanitarian aid once disaster strikes a poorer country.
Band 8: Donor nations are widely held to bear a moral obligation to mobilise humanitarian aid in the wake of catastrophe, not least because global prosperity is so unevenly distributed.
2. Band 7: Some powerful figures are rarely held accountable for the crimes they commit.
Band 8: Powerful figures all too often act with impunity, shielded from accountability by the very institutions meant to restrain them.
3. Band 7: Excessive reliance on foreign aid can gradually undermine a country's own economic capacity.
Band 8: Protracted aid dependency can inadvertently erode a nation's capacity for self-reliance, trapping it in a cycle that is difficult to escape.
4. Band 7: Countries need to cooperate on a multilateral basis for international agreements to be effective.
Band 8: Multilateral treaties, once ratified, establish a binding framework that lends international cooperation far greater legitimacy than any single state acting alone.
5. Band 7: Economic sanctions are frequently imposed to pressure governments into changing their policies.

Band 8: Economic sanctions are routinely wielded as a coercive instrument to compel changes in state behaviour, though their humanitarian repercussions are seldom proportionate to the strategic gains.
6. Band 7: It is difficult to enforce international law properly when no single authority has overall control.
Band 8: International law's fundamental weakness lies in the absence of a supreme authority to compel compliance, leaving enforcement to rest on reputational pressure and sanctions alone.
7. Band 7: Aid organisations should be transparent about how donated funds are allocated and spent.
Band 8: Humanitarian organisations can only sustain public trust by demonstrating rigorous accountability over how every donated fund is allocated.
8. Band 7: Outside intervention in another nation's conflict should only be considered in the most extreme circumstances.
Band 8: Humanitarian intervention should be reserved for cases where atrocity crimes are imminent and every diplomatic remedy has been exhausted, lest sovereignty be eroded on flimsy pretexts.

2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: International Aid vs. Domestic Spending (Charity begins at home)

Arguments for Domestic Priority: Governments collect taxes to serve their own citizens first; solving domestic issues like homelessness and crumbling infrastructure should take absolute precedence over foreign crises.

Arguments for International Aid: We live in an interconnected global village—a catastrophe abroad (e.g., a pandemic or war) inevitably creates refugee waves and economic repercussions at home; providing aid fulfills a fundamental moral obligation of wealthy nations.
Topic: Does Foreign Aid Create Dependency?

The Dependency Trap: Endless shipments of free food and clothing can bankrupt local farmers and businesses who cannot compete with "free" goods, creating a vicious cycle of reliance on foreign handouts.

The Empowerment Solution: Aid must shift from mere "relief" to "development." By allocating funds to build schools, hospitals, and agricultural training, aid can empower nations to achieve self-sufficiency.
Topic: The Effectiveness of Economic Sanctions
Arguments FOR Sanctions: A non-violent diplomatic tool to pressure rogue regimes into abandoning human rights violations or nuclear programmes without resorting to military warfare.

Arguments AGAINST Sanctions: Dictators rarely suffer from embargoes; instead, the severe economic repercussions disproportionately harm innocent civilians by causing hyperinflation and medicine shortages.

Model Answer (≈ 271 words, Band 7.5–8.0):

The international issue that weighs on me most heavily is climate-induced displacement — what the UNHCR has begun classifying as "climate refugees", a category that currently encompasses an estimated 21.5 million people annually since 2008. What makes this crisis particularly insidious is that it sits in a legal grey zone: those fleeing rising sea levels or desertification do not qualify for protection under the 1951 Refugee Convention, which only recognises persecution-based claims. It is precisely this lacuna in international law that I find ethically untenable.

I first became aware of the issue through a Doctors Without Borders documentary on the Sahel, where prolonged droughts have triggered mass migration into already-fragile coastal states. What struck me was the cascading nature of the catastrophe: ecological collapse begets economic ruin, which begets political instability, which in turn fuels conflict.

In terms of remedial action, multilateral efforts have been frankly underwhelming. The Loss and Damage Fund, ratified at COP28, was a symbolic breakthrough — yet pledges thus far amount to under a billion dollars, a drop in the ocean against estimated needs of several hundred billion. Some progressive jurisdictions, notably New Zealand, have piloted humanitarian visas for Pacific Island climate migrants, but such initiatives remain the exception.

Why does it matter to me personally? Vietnam's Mekong Delta — home to nearly twenty million people — is projected to be largely submerged by 2050 under current trajectories. So this isn't an abstract issue confined to distant coastlines; it's an existential threat to my own region. Were the international community to grant climate refugees formal legal status, what would follow is not charity but the discharge of a moral obligation owed to those bearing the brunt of others' emissions.

sections.title: PART 2 — Describe an international issue you care about

blocks.text: Q1: Should the United Nations have more enforcement power?

I lean cautiously in favour, though I recognise the constitutional and political obstacles are formidable. The current UN architecture is, in many respects, structurally hamstrung — the Security Council veto routinely paralyses action on humanitarian catastrophes, as we've seen in Syria, Yemen and Gaza. What strengthening UN authority might look like is a reformed Security Council with restricted veto rights for atrocity crimes, coupled with a standing rapid-reaction force funded through assessed contributions. That said, I'm wary of unchecked supranational power; sovereignty remains the bedrock of the Westphalian order, and any erosion of it must be carefully circumscribed. The pragmatic middle path, I think, is incremental empowerment within the framework of jus cogens norms — those peremptory rules like the prohibitions on genocide and torture that no state can lawfully derogate from. Beyond that, expanding UN authority risks legitimacy backlash from emerging powers.
Q2: Is humanitarian intervention ever justified?

This is genuinely one of the thorniest questions in international relations, and I'd answer with a heavily qualified yes. The Responsibility to Protect doctrine, endorsed at the 2005 World Summit, establishes that sovereignty entails obligations — and where a state manifestly fails to protect its population from mass atrocities, the international community has a moral duty to act. Rwanda 1994 stands as the haunting counterfactual: had the UN intervened decisively, perhaps 800,000 lives would have been spared. However, the post-2011 Libyan operation illustrates how interventions can spiral into protracted instability if exit strategies are absent. So while I accept the principle, the threshold must be exceptionally high: imminent mass atrocities, exhaustion of diplomatic remedies, multilateral authorisation, and a credible reconstruction plan. Anything short of that risks weaponising humanitarianism as a Trojan horse for geopolitical agendas.
Q3: How can international law actually be enforced when there's no global police?

This is the fundamental Achilles' heel of the international legal order — there's no Leviathan to compel compliance. What enforcement does exist operates through three imperfect mechanisms: reputational costs, economic sanctions and, in extreme cases, collective security action. Reputational pressure works surprisingly well for democracies sensitive to soft-power optics, but it largely fails against authoritarian regimes. Sanctions, meanwhile, have a chequered track record; the literature suggests they succeed roughly 30% of the time, and the humanitarian repercussions for civilians often outweigh the strategic gains. What I think would genuinely move the needle is universal jurisdiction for atrocity crimes — empowering domestic courts to prosecute perpetrators regardless of nationality — alongside strengthened ICC capacity. Ultimately, though, international law functions less as enforceable command and more as normative gravity, gradually shaping state behaviour through socialisation and habit.

1. Section Type

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Welcome back. Today's lecture probes the perennial tension between three pillars of public international law: humanitarian intervention, the sovereignty doctrine and customary international law. The Westphalian settlement of 1648, I shall argue, has been substantially renegotiated.

> Let us begin with the sovereignty doctrine. Article 2(4) of the United Nations Charter prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity of any state. Yet the doctrine is no longer treated as inviolable. The 2005 World Summit Outcome enshrined the Responsibility to Protect — usually abbreviated R2P — which holds that sovereignty entails duties, not merely privileges. Where a state perpetrates atrocity crimes against its own population, that protective sovereignty lapses.

> Now, humanitarian intervention. The legal scholar Anne-Marie Slaughter has long argued that the NATO bombing of Kosovo in 1999 — "illegal but legitimate", in the Independent Commission's formulation — exposed an irreducible gap between law and morality. The Libya intervention of 2011 invoked R2P explicitly under Security Council Resolution 1973. Critics counter that R2P has been weaponised as a pretext for regime change, eroding consent for future interventions.

> Finally, customary international law. Unlike treaties, custom binds through two elements: consistent state practice and opinio juris — the belief that the practice is legally obligatory. The Nicaragua judgment of the International Court of Justice in 1986 reaffirmed customary prohibitions on the use of force. Certain norms — the prohibition of genocide, torture and slavery — achieve jus cogens status, from which no derogation is ever permitted.

Now, that catalogue of intervention precedents in table three will look, at first glance, like a record of progress — sovereignty yielding gracefully to conscience. I want to disturb that reading, because the very same precedents sustain a powerful counter-narrative, and a serious student of international law must hold both at once. The objection comes, tellingly, not from the global North but from the global South. [pause] Many post-colonial states regard the entire R2P apparatus with deep suspicion, reading it as a juridical reincarnation of the "civilising mission" — a doctrine through which powerful states arrogate to themselves the right to police the weak, never the reverse.

And the selectivity problem gives that suspicion real teeth. We intervened in Libya in 2011; we did not intervene, at remotely comparable scale, in Syria, despite atrocities of a far greater magnitude. Why? The cynical but largely accurate answer is the Security Council veto — the structural fact that intervention is licensed only where no permanent member's strategic interest objects. So the law, as applied, tracks great-power convenience rather than human suffering. That, um, is corrosive to the doctrine's legitimacy in a way no amount of high principle repairs.

There is a further wrinkle the Libya case crystallised. Resolution 1973 authorised the protection of civilians; what followed looked, to many states, like authorised regime change. The legal scholars call this mandate creep, and its consequence was concrete and lasting — Russia and China subsequently hardened their posture precisely because they felt the earlier authorisation had been exceeded. [pause] In other words, one expansive intervention can poison the well of consent for the next decade of genuine emergencies.

So we are left with a sobering trade-off: the more elastically we interpret humanitarian licence, the more we erode the collective trust on which any future licence depends. Which is exactly the tension the concluding section must adjudicate, as we ask whether…

> The synthesis is delicate: sovereignty must absorb humanitarian conscience without dissolving into selective enforcement. International law advances not through revolutions but through patient sedimentation. Now, turning to table three, which catalogues post-1990 intervention precedents…

The two pie charts illustrate how global humanitarian aid was distributed across seven sectors by major OECD donors in 2000 and 2024.

Overall, aid allocation underwent a pronounced reconfiguration: long-term development categories such as education and infrastructure contracted markedly, while climate- and health-related sectors expanded to dominate contemporary donor commitment. This suggests that aid has become increasingly reactive rather than developmental.

To begin with, climate adaptation surged sixfold from a marginal 3% to 18%, while disbursement to health and pandemic response climbed from 14% to 24%, overtaking food aid to become the single leading sector. Conversely, infrastructure and water funding plummeted from 18% to a mere 4%, the steepest fall of any category, while education's share contracted from 16% to 11%.

Meanwhile, the remaining sectors shifted only modestly. Emergency food and shelter, although still substantial, retreated from 28% to 22%, slipping from first to second place, and governance and anti-corruption funding eased slightly from 9% to 7%. By contrast, refugee and displacement assistance edged up from 12% to 14%, broadly consistent with the protracted displacement crises observed worldwide over the period.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~178 từ)
The two pie charts set out how major OECD donors apportioned global humanitarian aid across seven sectors in 2000 and 2024.

Overall, the humanitarian envelope underwent a striking reconfiguration: long-horizon development categories were sharply pared back, whereas climate- and health-related sectors swelled to dominate contemporary donor commitment. The pattern intimates a decisive pivot from developmental investment toward reactive crisis response.

The sharpest movements lay at the two extremes. Climate adaptation sextupled, leaping from a marginal 3% to 18%, while health and pandemic response climbed from 14% to 24%, displacing emergency food aid as the single largest recipient. This realignment arguably mirrors both post-pandemic priorities and intensifying climate commitments.

The declines were equally telling. Infrastructure and water collapsed from 18% to a negligible 4%, and education slid from 16% to 11%, as capital-intensive projects ceded ground to acute relief. Elsewhere, change was muted: emergency food and shelter eased from 28% to 22%, governance funding slipped to 7%, and refugee assistance edged up to 14% — the last broadly consistent with the protracted displacement crises that defined the intervening decades.

•  R2P (2005) ràng buộc chủ quyền vào nghĩa vụ bảo vệ dân; khi nghĩa vụ sụp đổ, cộng đồng quốc tế có trách nhiệm dư.
•  Trừng phạt có mục tiêu, gìn giữ hoà bình và áp lực đa phương có thể chặn tội ác mà không cần nổ súng.
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion
•  Introduction — diễn giải xung đột giữa chủ quyền và nhân quyền; luận điểm: chủ quyền là mặc định nhưng phải nhường trong trường hợp tội ác hàng loạt.
•  Body 1 — phía non-interference: chủ quyền giữ ổn định, can thiệp dễ bị lạm dụng và gây hậu quả cho dân thường.
•  Body 2 — phía can thiệp: chủ quyền không che chắn diệt chủng; R2P và công cụ đa phương cho phép hành động hợp pháp.
•  Conclusion — chủ quyền được bảo vệ trừ khi vi phạm jus cogens có hệ thống; can thiệp phải đa phương, tương xứng, vì dân thường.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~270 words)

Few questions in international relations are as contentious as whether the outside world should intervene when a government abuses its own people. While some insist that sovereignty is sacrosanct, others argue that universal human rights override territorial borders. My own view, with reservations, is that sovereignty should yield in cases of mass atrocity, although intervention must be tightly disciplined.

On one hand, defenders of strict non-interference tend to argue that respect for sovereignty is what keeps the international order stable. It is precisely because powerful states historically used 'humanitarian' pretexts to invade weaker ones that many developing nations remain deeply suspicious of intervention today. Furthermore, foreign military action, even when well-intentioned, often produces severe repercussions for civilians — refugee waves, embezzlement of relief funds and prolonged instability — outcomes that no donor country can fully control.

On the other hand, advocates of intervention point out that the doctrine of sovereignty was never meant to shield perpetrators of genocide or ethnic cleansing. When a regime turns its weapons on its own citizens, the international community has a moral obligation, arguably codified by the Responsibility to Protect, to step in. Targeted sanctions, peacekeeping missions and multilateral pressure can sometimes halt atrocities without firing a single shot, particularly when authorised by the UN Security Council.

In my view, sovereignty should be respected as the default rule, but it cannot be absolute when grave human rights violations are taking place. Provided that intervention is multilateral, proportionate and aimed at protecting civilians rather than regime change, the international community is justified in acting. Otherwise, sovereignty becomes a shield behind which dictators commit atrocities with impunity.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~289 words)

Humanitarian intervention sits uneasily at the intersection of two competing pillars of international order: the Westphalian principle of sovereignty and the post-1945 codification of universal human rights. While respect for sovereignty remains the default rule, it should, in my view, yield in narrowly defined circumstances where atrocities engage the realm of jus cogens norms.

Defenders of strict non-interference argue that sovereign equality is the load-bearing wall of the international system. Were it abandoned lightly, powerful states would, as history attests, repurpose 'humanitarian' rhetoric to justify regime change in geopolitically convenient locations. So consequential are these precedents that even well-intentioned action can erode trust in multilateral institutions for decades, particularly in the Global South. Moreover, coercive measures — comprehensive sanctions, no-fly zones, military strikes — frequently produce severe repercussions for the very civilians they purport to protect, while dictators absorb the political costs with relative ease.

By contrast, proponents of intervention contend that sovereignty was never designed to shield genocide, ethnic cleansing or crimes against humanity. The Responsibility to Protect doctrine, endorsed by the UN General Assembly in 2005, explicitly conditions sovereignty on a state's discharge of its duty to its population. Where that duty collapses, the international community arguably acquires a residual obligation, exercisable through targeted sanctions, peacekeeping operations and, as a last resort, multilateral force authorised by the Security Council.

My own position is that sovereignty deserves robust protection in ordinary politics but must give way when jus cogens prohibitions are breached on a systematic scale. Provided that intervention is multilaterally authorised, proportionate and tightly framed around civilian protection rather than regime engineering, it can be both lawful and legitimate. Beyond those guardrails, however, sovereignty must be respected, lest humanitarianism degenerate into a polite cover for great-power competition.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cú pháp cao cấp dày đặc (đảo ngữ điều kiện 'Were it abandoned lightly', đảo ngữ 'So consequential are these precedents', mệnh đề 'Where that duty collapses') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một vài lần.

•  Band 8 huy động lexis chuyên ngành luật quốc tế ('jus cogens', 'Westphalian sovereignty', 'residual obligation', 'regime engineering', 'no-fly zones') và dẫn mốc cụ thể (R2P 2005), nâng Lexical Resource và Task Response một bậc.

•  Band 8 đạt register học thuật nhất quán và cohesion tinh vi, loại bỏ cụm hơi đời thường như 'firing a single shot' / 'with impunity' ở cuối câu của Band 7, đồng thời khép bằng 'lest + subjunctive' sắc bén.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chủ quyền, quyền lực tối cao và độc lập của một quốc gia trong việc tự quản lý mình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Nations fiercely protect their **sovereignty**, making foreign intervention legally complex.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'sovereign' (quân vương tối cao) + -ty → quyền lực tối cao của một quốc gia, không ai can thiệp được.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'sovereignty' (chủ quyền, danh từ trừu tượng) với 'sovereign' (quốc vương, hoặc tính từ 'có chủ quyền').
vocabulary.definition_en: the supreme authority and independent power of a state to govern itself without outside interference
vocabulary.definition_vi: chủ quyền quốc gia
vocabulary.example: Nations fiercely protect their sovereignty, making foreign intervention legally complex.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'sovereign' (quân vương tối cao) + -ty → quyền lực tối cao của một quốc gia, không ai can thiệp được.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Lệnh trừng phạt, thường mang tính kinh tế, do một quốc gia hoặc tổ chức áp đặt lên quốc gia khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> When international bodies impose economic **sanctions** on a rogue state to force compliance, it can have devastating repercussions on the innocent civilian population.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Nghĩ tới 'sanction' như một 'lệnh' chính thức từ trên xuống → khi ở số nhiều, đó là loạt lệnh trừng phạt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Sanction' số ít có thể là động từ (chấp thuận) hoặc danh từ (sự cho phép); nghĩa 'trừng phạt' luôn dùng số nhiều 'sanctions'.
vocabulary.definition_en: penalties, typically economic, imposed by one country or body on another to coerce a change in behaviour
vocabulary.definition_vi: lệnh trừng phạt (thường là kinh tế)
vocabulary.example: When international bodies impose economic sanctions on a rogue state to force compliance, it can have devastating repercussions on the innocent civilian population.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Nghĩ tới 'sanction' như một 'lệnh' chính thức từ trên xuống → khi ở số nhiều, đó là loạt lệnh trừng phạt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hành vi biển thủ hoặc chiếm đoạt trái phép tiền/tài sản được giao phó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> In regimes with weak governance, the **embezzlement** of foreign funds by corrupt leaders is a rampant issue.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'em-' + 'bezzle' nghe như 'puzzle' tiền bạc bị biến mất một cách khó hiểu → biển thủ công quỹ.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Embezzlement' chỉ áp dụng cho tiền/tài sản được GIAO PHÓ hợp pháp rồi bị chiếm đoạt, khác với 'theft' (trộm cắp thông thường).
vocabulary.definition_en: the theft or misappropriation of funds placed in one's trust or under one's official control
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự biển thủ, tham ô công quỹ
vocabulary.example: In regimes with weak governance, the embezzlement of foreign funds by corrupt leaders is a rampant issue.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'em-' + 'bezzle' nghe như 'puzzle' tiền bạc bị biến mất một cách khó hiểu → biển thủ công quỹ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đa phương, có sự tham gia của ba bên (thường là quốc gia) trở lên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many countries working together through **multilateral** cooperation is the only way to solve this.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'multi-' (nhiều) + 'lateral' (bên, phía) → nhiều phía cùng tham gia.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'multilateral' (nhiều bên, 3+) với 'bilateral' (song phương, 2 bên) và 'unilateral' (đơn phương, 1 bên).
vocabulary.definition_en: involving three or more parties, especially countries, typically referring to treaties or agreements
vocabulary.definition_vi: đa phương (liên quan từ ba bên trở lên)
vocabulary.example: Many countries working together through multilateral cooperation is the only way to solve this.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'multi-' (nhiều) + 'lateral' (bên, phía) → nhiều phía cùng tham gia.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mang tính nhân đạo, hướng tới việc thúc đẩy phúc lợi và giảm bớt khổ đau của con người.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Donor nations routinely mobilise **humanitarian** aid in the wake of natural catastrophes.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'human' (con người) + -itarian → người đặt phúc lợi con người lên hàng đầu → nhân đạo.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'humanitarian' (mang tính nhân đạo, liên quan cứu trợ) với 'humane' (nhân từ, đối xử tử tế nói chung).
vocabulary.definition_en: concerned with promoting human welfare, especially through the relief of suffering
vocabulary.definition_vi: mang tính nhân đạo
vocabulary.example: Donor nations routinely mobilise humanitarian aid in the wake of natural catastrophes.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'human' (con người) + -itarian → người đặt phúc lợi con người lên hàng đầu → nhân đạo.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ký hoặc chính thức chấp thuận một hiệp ước, hợp đồng, khiến nó có hiệu lực pháp lý.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Multilateral treaties, once **ratified**, establish a binding framework for international cooperation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'rat-' gợi 'rate' (đánh giá, phê) + '-ify' (làm cho) → làm cho có hiệu lực chính thức bằng cách phê chuẩn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Ratify' mang tính chính thức, mức độ pháp lý cao hơn 'agree to' hay 'sign' thông thường; đối tượng thường là 'treaty/agreement', không phải người.
vocabulary.definition_en: to sign or give formal, official consent to a treaty, contract or agreement, making it legally valid
vocabulary.definition_vi: phê chuẩn (một hiệp ước, thoả thuận)
vocabulary.example: Multilateral treaties, once ratified, establish a binding framework for international cooperation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'rat-' gợi 'rate' (đánh giá, phê) + '-ify' (làm cho) → làm cho có hiệu lực chính thức bằng cách phê chuẩn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trao quyền, năng lực hoặc sự tự tin để ai đó có thể tự hành động, tự lực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> By allocating funds to build schools, hospitals and agricultural training, aid can **empower** nations to achieve self-sufficiency.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'em-' (làm cho) + 'power' (quyền lực) → trao quyền lực cho ai đó tự đứng vững.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Empower' cần tân ngữ (empower someone TO DO something); tránh dùng như tính từ ('empower' không phải là adj, phải dùng 'empowered').
vocabulary.definition_en: to give someone the authority, power or confidence to do something, especially to act independently
vocabulary.definition_vi: trao quyền, tiếp sức cho ai đó tự lực
vocabulary.example: By allocating funds to build schools, hospitals and agricultural training, aid can empower nations to achieve self-sufficiency.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'em-' (làm cho) + 'power' (quyền lực) → trao quyền lực cho ai đó tự đứng vững.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phân bổ nguồn lực hoặc nhiệm vụ cho một mục đích, nhóm người cụ thể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Donors must carefully **allocate** their resources to ensure they reach the intended beneficiaries.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'al-' + 'locate' (định vị/đặt vào chỗ) → đặt nguồn lực vào đúng chỗ cần thiết → phân bổ.
vocabulary.common_error: Cấu trúc chuẩn là 'allocate sth TO sb/sth', đừng dùng nhầm giới từ 'for'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to distribute resources or duties for a particular purpose to particular people or causes
vocabulary.definition_vi: phân bổ (nguồn lực, ngân sách)
vocabulary.example: Donors must carefully allocate their resources to ensure they reach the intended beneficiaries.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'al-' + 'locate' (định vị/đặt vào chỗ) → đặt nguồn lực vào đúng chỗ cần thiết → phân bổ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trách nhiệm giải trình, nghĩa vụ phải chịu trách nhiệm và giải thích cho hành động của mình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> International **accountability** mechanisms are essential to ensure that aid money is not embezzled by corrupt officials.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'account' (giải trình, sổ sách) + -ability → khả năng phải giải trình cho hành động của mình.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Accountability' (danh từ trừu tượng, không đếm được) khác với 'account' (tài khoản/bản tường trình); tính từ tương ứng là 'accountable', không phải 'accountability' + adj.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of being responsible for one's actions and required to explain or justify them
vocabulary.definition_vi: trách nhiệm giải trình
vocabulary.example: International accountability mechanisms are essential to ensure that aid money is not embezzled by corrupt officials.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'account' (giải trình, sổ sách) + -ability → khả năng phải giải trình cho hành động của mình.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự lệ thuộc kéo dài, đặc biệt là vào viện trợ nước ngoài, làm giảm khả năng tự lực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Protracted aid **dependency** can inadvertently undermine a nation's capacity for self-reliance.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'depend' (phụ thuộc) + -ency → trạng thái phụ thuộc kéo dài, khó tự đứng vững.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Dependency' và 'dependence' gần như đồng nghĩa, nhưng 'dependency' thường dùng cho hiện tượng mang tính hệ thống/dài hạn (aid dependency), còn 'dependence' phổ biến hơn ở nghĩa cá nhân.
vocabulary.definition_en: the state of relying heavily on someone or something else, especially in a way that limits self-sufficiency
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự lệ thuộc (đặc biệt vào viện trợ nước ngoài)
vocabulary.example: Protracted aid dependency can inadvertently undermine a nation's capacity for self-reliance.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'depend' (phụ thuộc) + -ency → trạng thái phụ thuộc kéo dài, khó tự đứng vững.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thẩm quyền tài phán, quyền lực chính thức để áp dụng luật pháp hoặc đưa ra phán quyết.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Universal **jurisdiction** empowers domestic courts to prosecute perpetrators of atrocity crimes regardless of nationality.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'juris-' (luật) + 'diction' (nói/tuyên bố) → quyền tuyên bố phán quyết theo luật.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Jurisdiction' là quyền tài phán (thẩm quyền pháp lý), không phải 'jurisdiction' = toà án; đừng nhầm với 'jury' (bồi thẩm đoàn).
vocabulary.definition_en: the official power or legal authority to make judgements, apply laws or exercise control over a territory or people
vocabulary.definition_vi: thẩm quyền tài phán
vocabulary.example: Universal jurisdiction empowers domestic courts to prosecute perpetrators of atrocity crimes regardless of nationality.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'juris-' (luật) + 'diction' (nói/tuyên bố) → quyền tuyên bố phán quyết theo luật.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình trạng không bị trừng phạt hoặc không phải chịu hậu quả cho hành vi sai trái của mình.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Powerful figures all too often act with **impunity**, beyond the reach of international law.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'im-' (không) + 'punity' liên hệ 'punish' (trừng phạt) → không bị trừng phạt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Impunity' (thoát tội, không bị trừng phạt) dễ nhầm với 'immunity' (miễn trừ/miễn dịch); hai từ có nguồn gốc khác nhau dù nghĩa gần nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: exemption from punishment or from the negative consequences of one's actions
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự không bị trừng phạt, thoát tội
vocabulary.example: Powerful figures all too often act with impunity, beyond the reach of international law.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'im-' (không) + 'punity' liên hệ 'punish' (trừng phạt) → không bị trừng phạt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trách nhiệm Bảo vệ, học thuyết quốc tế năm 2005 cho phép can thiệp khi một quốc gia không bảo vệ được người dân của mình khỏi tội ác tày trời.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The 2005 World Summit Outcome enshrined the **Responsibility to Protect**, which holds that sovereignty entails duties, not merely privileges.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
responsibility (trách nhiệm) + to protect (để bảo vệ) → chủ quyền đi kèm nghĩa vụ bảo vệ dân, không phải đặc quyền tuyệt đối.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn viết hoa như một danh từ riêng chỉ học thuyết pháp lý cụ thể; viết tắt chuẩn là 'R2P', không phải 'RtP' hay 'R2p'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the 2005 international doctrine, often abbreviated R2P, permitting intervention when a state fails to protect its own population from atrocity crimes
vocabulary.definition_vi: Trách nhiệm Bảo vệ (học thuyết R2P, cho phép can thiệp khi nhà nước không bảo vệ được người dân)
vocabulary.example: The 2005 World Summit Outcome enshrined the Responsibility to Protect, which holds that sovereignty entails duties, not merely privileges.
vocabulary.memory_hook: responsibility (trách nhiệm) + to protect (để bảo vệ) → chủ quyền đi kèm nghĩa vụ bảo vệ dân, không phải đặc quyền tuyệt đối.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vật lộn, cố gắng giải quyết hoặc thấu hiểu một vấn đề khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Policymakers continue to **grapple with** the ethical dilemma of humanitarian intervention versus national sovereignty.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'grapple' gợi hình ảnh vật lộn tay đôi (grappling) → vật lộn với một vấn đề khó.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Grapple with' luôn đi kèm giới từ 'with'; không dùng 'grapple a problem' thiếu giới từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try hard to deal with or understand a difficult problem or issue
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn, nỗ lực giải quyết (một vấn đề khó khăn)
vocabulary.example: Policymakers continue to grapple with the ethical dilemma of humanitarian intervention versus national sovereignty.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grapple' gợi hình ảnh vật lộn tay đôi (grappling) → vật lộn với một vấn đề khó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tội ác tày trời, nhóm các tội danh nghiêm trọng nhất theo luật quốc tế như diệt chủng, tội ác chiến tranh và tội ác chống nhân loại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Where a state perpetrates **atrocity crimes** against its own population, that protective sovereignty lapses under the Responsibility to Protect doctrine.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
atrocity (sự tàn bạo) + crimes (tội ác) → nhóm tội ác nghiêm trọng nhất mà luật quốc tế trừng phạt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Atrocity crimes' là thuật ngữ pháp lý quốc tế bao hàm ba loại tội danh cụ thể (genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity), không dùng chung chung để chỉ 'hành vi tàn bạo' thông thường.
vocabulary.definition_en: the most serious international crimes, typically genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity
vocabulary.definition_vi: tội ác tày trời (diệt chủng, tội ác chiến tranh, tội ác chống nhân loại)
vocabulary.example: Where a state perpetrates atrocity crimes against its own population, that protective sovereignty lapses under the Responsibility to Protect doctrine.
vocabulary.memory_hook: atrocity (sự tàn bạo) + crimes (tội ác) → nhóm tội ác nghiêm trọng nhất mà luật quốc tế trừng phạt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Một vấn đề gây ra nhiều tranh cãi, bất đồng quan điểm gay gắt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Few questions in international relations are as **contentious** as whether the outside world should intervene when a government abuses its own people.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'contend' (tranh luận) + -ious → mang tính tranh cãi, gây bất đồng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Contentious' (gây tranh cãi) khác với 'content' (nội dung/hài lòng); trọng âm và nghĩa hoàn toàn khác nhau dù hình thức gần giống.
vocabulary.definition_en: a topic that causes strong disagreement or heated debate between people with opposing views
vocabulary.definition_vi: vấn đề gây nhiều tranh cãi
vocabulary.example: Few questions in international relations are as contentious as whether the outside world should intervene when a government abuses its own people.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'contend' (tranh luận) + -ious → mang tính tranh cãi, gây bất đồng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Được trao tặng hoặc thực hiện mà không kèm theo bất kỳ điều kiện ràng buộc nào.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The financial donation was given with **no strings attached**, allowing the charity to use it freely.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Món quà "không có dây (string) buộc" → cho đi mà không ràng buộc điều kiện gì.
collocations: give money with no strings attached
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm này luôn ở dạng bị động 'be given/come with no strings attached'; không chia động từ 'string' theo nghĩa này.
vocabulary.definition_en: given or done without any conditions or obligations imposed in return
vocabulary.definition_vi: không kèm điều kiện ràng buộc
vocabulary.example: The financial donation was given with no strings attached, allowing the charity to use it freely.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Món quà 'không có dây (string) buộc' → cho đi mà không ràng buộc điều kiện gì.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chủ động đưa ra cử chỉ hoà giải, làm hoà với đối thủ hoặc kẻ thù cũ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The president decided to **extend an olive branch** to the opposition party to start peace talks.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Cành ô liu (olive branch) là biểu tượng hoà bình từ thời cổ đại → chìa cành ô liu ra là chủ động làm hoà.
vocabulary.common_error: Động từ đi kèm chuẩn là 'extend' hoặc 'offer', không phải 'give' hay 'send' một cành ô liu.
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a gesture of peace or reconciliation towards someone, especially a former rival or enemy
vocabulary.definition_vi: đưa ra cành ô liu, chủ động làm hoà
vocabulary.example: The president decided to extend an olive branch to the opposition party to start peace talks.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Cành ô liu (olive branch) là biểu tượng hoà bình từ thời cổ đại → chìa cành ô liu ra là chủ động làm hoà.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quan điểm cho rằng nên chăm lo cho gia đình/đất nước mình trước khi giúp đỡ người khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Some critics argue we shouldn't send aid abroad because **charity begins at home**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'charity' (từ thiện) 'begins at home' (bắt đầu từ nhà) → giúp người nhà trước khi giúp người ngoài.
collocations: argue that charity begins at home
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là tục ngữ cố định, không chia động từ hay đổi trật tự từ; thường dùng để mở đầu lập luận phản đối viện trợ nước ngoài.
vocabulary.definition_en: the idea that one should first take care of one's own family or country before helping others
vocabulary.definition_vi: nên lo cho người thân/đất nước mình trước khi giúp người ngoài
vocabulary.example: Some critics argue we shouldn't send aid abroad because charity begins at home.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'charity' (từ thiện) 'begins at home' (bắt đầu từ nhà) → giúp người nhà trước khi giúp người ngoài.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cố gắng giải quyết một vấn đề chỉ bằng cách chi thật nhiều tiền, mà thiếu chiến lược bài bản.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> You can't just **throw money at** the problem; we need a long-term sustainable strategy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình ảnh "ném" (throw) tiền một cách hú hoạ vào vấn đề → chi tiền mà không có kế hoạch rõ ràng.
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm này mang hàm ý phê phán (thiếu chiến lược), không dùng để khen ngợi việc chi tiêu hào phóng.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try to solve a problem simply by spending large amounts of money on it, without a proper strategy
vocabulary.definition_vi: ném tiền vào giải quyết vấn đề (một cách thiếu chiến lược)
vocabulary.example: You can't just throw money at the problem; we need a long-term sustainable strategy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình ảnh 'ném' (throw) tiền một cách hú hoạ vào vấn đề → chi tiền mà không có kế hoạch rõ ràng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bị ràng buộc, không thể tự do hành động do quy định hoặc hoàn cảnh ngoài tầm kiểm soát.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> I would love to help the refugees cross the border, but my **hands are tied** by international regulations.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình ảnh đôi tay bị trói (tied) lại → không thể tự do hành động dù muốn.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn chia ở dạng bị động 'hands are/were tied'; không nói 'tie my hands' để diễn tả trạng thái bị ràng buộc hiện tại.
vocabulary.definition_en: to be prevented from acting freely because of rules, regulations or circumstances beyond one's control
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị trói tay, không thể tự do hành động (do quy định, hoàn cảnh)
vocabulary.example: I would love to help the refugees cross the border, but my hands are tied by international regulations.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình ảnh đôi tay bị trói (tied) lại → không thể tự do hành động dù muốn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Câu chữ máy móc, nghĩa đen của luật pháp, trái ngược với tinh thần thực sự của nó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The cruel judge followed the strict **letter of the law**, completely ignoring the spirit of it.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'letter' (chữ cái) của luật → áp dụng luật theo đúng từng chữ, máy móc, bỏ qua ý nghĩa sâu xa.
collocations: follow the letter of the law
the letter versus the spirit of the law
stick to the letter of the law
vocabulary.common_error: Thường xuất hiện đối lập với 'the spirit of the law' (tinh thần của luật); tránh dùng tách rời khỏi ngữ cảnh so sánh này.
vocabulary.definition_en: the precise, literal wording of a law or rule, as opposed to its underlying intention or spirit
vocabulary.definition_vi: câu chữ máy móc của luật (khác với tinh thần của luật)
vocabulary.example: The cruel judge followed the strict letter of the law, completely ignoring the spirit of it.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'letter' (chữ cái) của luật → áp dụng luật theo đúng từng chữ, máy móc, bỏ qua ý nghĩa sâu xa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bôi trơn để một việc diễn ra suôn sẻ hơn, thường ngầm ám chỉ việc hối lộ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> In some deeply corrupt nations, foreign businesses have to **grease the wheels** to get permits approved.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Bánh xe (wheels) chạy trơn tru hơn khi được "bôi trơn" (grease) → dùng tiền/quà để việc chạy suôn sẻ, ám chỉ hối lộ.
collocations: grease the wheels to get sth done
vocabulary.common_error: Trong ngữ cảnh luật pháp/tham nhũng, cụm này thường hàm ý hối lộ tế nhị hơn từ 'bribe' trực diện; cần cẩn trọng khi dùng trong văn phong học thuật trang trọng.
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a process happen more smoothly or quickly, often by offering money or favours, sometimes implying bribery
vocabulary.definition_vi: bôi trơn (thường ám chỉ hối lộ để việc trôi chảy hơn)
vocabulary.example: In some deeply corrupt nations, foreign businesses have to grease the wheels to get permits approved.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Bánh xe (wheels) chạy trơn tru hơn khi được 'bôi trơn' (grease) → dùng tiền/quà để việc chạy suôn sẻ, ám chỉ hối lộ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cố tình làm ngơ, không muốn thừa nhận một điều sai trái mà mình biết rõ đang xảy ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Sadly, many powerful countries simply **turn a blind eye** to human rights abuses if it benefits their trade.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Nhắm một mắt lại' (turn a blind eye) khi nhìn thấy điều sai → cố tình lờ đi, không muốn can thiệp.
collocations: turn a blind eye to abuses
refuse to turn a blind eye
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm cố định luôn dùng giới từ 'to' theo sau ('turn a blind eye TO sth'), không dùng 'turn a blind eye on/for'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to deliberately ignore or refuse to acknowledge something wrong that one knows is happening
vocabulary.definition_vi: làm ngơ, cố tình không thấy (điều sai trái)
vocabulary.example: Sadly, many powerful countries simply turn a blind eye to human rights abuses if it benefits their trade.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Nhắm một mắt lại' (turn a blind eye) khi nhìn thấy điều sai → cố tình lờ đi, không muốn can thiệp.
